title: Samsung and SK Hynix Race for ASML’s Scarce EUV Machines
gist: Samsung and SK Hynix are each reportedly committing ~$6.7–13.3B to ASML EUV tools and pulling orders forward as lead times double; ASML says planned capacity won't fully meet 2027 or 2028 demand. The author argues tool delivery timing is becoming a competitive advantage that will gate memory supply for AI infrastructure.

insights.claim: Samsung and SK Hynix are each reportedly committing roughly $6.7 billion to $13.3 billion to ASML extreme ultraviolet lithography equipment and are considering placing future orders earlier to secure delivery slots.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Signals a multi-year EUV order backlog from memory makers, supportive for ASML bookings into 2027–2028.

insights.claim: SK Hynix has disclosed an ASML equipment purchase worth about $8 billion with delivery scheduled by December 31, 2027.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Hard, disclosed order that underpins SK Hynix's capacity ramp timeline through 2027.

insights.claim: Samsung has reportedly ordered lithography equipment for its Pyeongtaek P5 development, where investment is expected to exceed about $40 billion per fab.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: P5 scale implies large equipment spend flowing to lithography and other WFE vendors.

insights.claim: ASML said in its October results that its currently planned capacity would not fully satisfy customer demand in 2027 or 2028, and it is exploring expansion beyond previously discussed capacity increases.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: EUV is supply-constrained for two years — supports ASML pricing power and further capacity capex.
insights.quote: its currently planned capacity would not fully satisfy customer demand in either 2027 or 2028

insights.claim: ASML equipment lead times are reportedly doubling, pushing chipmakers to order earlier to secure delivery slots.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Longer lead times pull orders forward, lifting ASML near-term bookings but raising later cancellation/air-pocket risk.
insights.locator: With equipment lead times reportedly doubling

insights.claim: Delivery timing of lithography tools is becoming a competitive advantage: a chipmaker can finance a fab and finish its cleanroom, but output depends on equipment being installed, qualified and running reliably.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Favor memory makers with secured EUV slots; tool-starved fabs risk stranded capex while rivals ramp.
insights.quote: My assessment is that delivery timing is becoming a competitive advantage.

insights.claim: Delayed EUV tools could leave expensive memory-fab infrastructure idle while competitors move ahead, whereas earlier securing protects technology roadmaps and accelerates capacity additions.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Watch relative EUV install schedules between Samsung and SK Hynix as a leading indicator of memory share shifts.
insights.locator: For Samsung and SK Hynix, securing those machines

insights.claim: The key strategic question in memory is which company can convert enormous spending commitments into qualified production capacity first.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Track qualified-capacity milestones, not capex headlines, to judge winners.
insights.quote: who can turn enormous spending commitments into qualified production capacity first?
insights.locator: The strategic question is becoming clear

themes.theme: AI memory supply and capital risk

insights.claim: EUV equipment shortages could influence how quickly additional memory supply reaches the AI infrastructure market, though yields, packaging capacity and customer qualification will also shape outcomes.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: EUV scarcity may prolong tight AI memory supply, supporting memory pricing.
insights.locator: The implications extend to AI infrastructure

insights.claim: Ordering EUV tools earlier forces chipmakers to commit capital further ahead of actual production needs, increasing exposure if demand changes.
insights.speaker: SemiWiki
insights.so_what: Pulled-forward capex raises downside risk for memory makers and ASML order durability if AI demand softens.
insights.locator: There is a financial tradeoff, too
